issues.subcategory: retrospective episode ascertainment mislabeled as prospective
issues.description: The study repeatedly characterizes its design as prospective or as enabling real-time/dynamic assessment, but the core design is retrospective: participants retrospectively identified past episodes and the investigators then linked archived texts to those recalled windows. This matters because recall error, post-hoc reconstruction, and outcome knowledge can bias episode boundaries and classifications, undermining claims about prospective prediction or real-time identification.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: predictive/real-time claims from retrospective correlational data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly implies that the findings identify real-time markers and could determine when someone is at imminent risk, but the analyses are retrospective associations between recalled episode windows and text features. No prospective validation, out-of-sample prediction, or temporal intervention framework is presented. The results therefore do not establish real-time identification or prediction of suicide risk.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: episode misclassification due to nonstandard attempt definition
issues.description: The study collapses actual, interrupted, and aborted attempts into one 'suicide attempt episode,' and even includes incidents with no enacted self-harm based on participants' subjective endorsement. This severely broadens and destabilizes the outcome construct, mixing phenomenologically and clinically distinct states. Such heterogeneity can bias associations and weakens interpretability of any 'attempt-specific' findings.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”... reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt

issues.subcategory: social engagement operationalized as message volume ratio
issues.description: The manuscript claims to assess social engagement, thwarted belongingness, and burdensomeness using only ratios/counts of sent versus received messages. Message volume is a weak and indirect proxy for these interpersonal constructs and may reflect many unrelated factors (phone use habits, recipient behavior, logistics, academic workload). This threatens construct validity and makes theoretical interpretation inappropriate.
issues.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

issues.subcategory: self-focus operationalized narrowly by first-person singular pronouns
issues.description: The study equates self-focus with first-person singular pronoun use. While common in LIWC-based work, this is only a partial and contested proxy for self-focus and may reflect ordinary conversational style, texting conventions, or grammar rather than maladaptive self-attention. The manuscript treats this operationalization as if it directly indexes the theoretical construct.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of self-focus) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: sentiment/emotion categories do not map cleanly onto suicide-related affective constructs
issues.description: The study infers depressed affect, hopelessness, anxiety, and related risk states from LIWC single-word categories. But the chosen variables do not directly measure hopelessness, suicidal intent, agitation, or other acute-risk constructs, and LIWC is context-insensitive. This mismatch limits the extent to which findings can be interpreted as evidence about the theorized emotional mechanisms of suicide risk.
issues.quote: Language analysis software scored 189,478 text messages to capture three psychological constructs: self-focus, sentiment, and social engagement.

issues.subcategory: selection bias from requiring retrievable historical text data
issues.description: Eligibility depended on having accessible historical messaging data dating back before key life events. This likely selected for younger, more technologically consistent, and less socioeconomically diverse participants, and may also be associated with communication habits or psychopathology. Such selection bias may distort associations and limits representativeness.
issues.quote: Inclusion criteria included... availability of and access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events (e.g., suicide attempt)

issues.subcategory: highly restricted sample
issues.description: The sample is predominantly female, White, college-aged, and partially drawn from a psychology participant pool. The findings should not be generalized to broader clinical populations, older adults, men, non-college populations, individuals with severe psychopathology, or suicide decedents. Although some of this is acknowledged later, the framing often implies broader applicability than the sample supports.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.subcategory: exclusion of currently high-risk individuals
issues.description: Participants at high or imminent current risk were excluded, yet the paper is framed around identifying imminent suicide risk. Excluding individuals who are currently most clinically relevant may systematically remove those with the strongest acute-risk signals and reduces applicability to real-world imminent-risk detection.
issues.quote: Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior... were excluded from study participation

issues.subcategory: substantial missing episode/text data not addressed analytically
issues.description: Less than half of elicited episodes had SMS data, and only 27 of 33 participants contributed any messaging episodes; only 15 participants had attempt episodes with SMS data. This is not just routine missingness but highly selective availability of the primary data. The manuscript does not assess whether episodes/participants with versus without SMS data differed systematically, nor whether missingness is plausibly ignorable.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants. Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: inappropriate implication that mixed models solve nonrandom missingness
issues.description: The manuscript presents mixed-effects models as able to 'handle missing data' in this context, but mixed models do not eliminate bias from missing-not-at-random episode availability or selective data recovery. Because SMS retrieval depended on device history, backups, and technical factors possibly related to participant characteristics, the missing data mechanism may be nonignorable.
issues.quote: A mixed-effects method was selected because of its well-established advantages in terms of producing more accurate effect estimates and its ability to handle missing data... especially appropriate for this dataset given the amount of ‘missing data’

issues.subcategory: incorrect test statistic notation for chi-square
issues.description: Throughout the results tables/text, chi-square statistics are reported as '2(3)=...' rather than the standard χ²(3)=.... This suggests either a formatting loss or reporting error. While notation alone is minor, it impedes interpretation and raises concern about care in statistical reporting.
issues.quote: there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.033.

issues.subcategory: contradictory interpretation of significant pairwise slope comparisons
issues.description: For self-focus, the pairwise comparisons show significant attempt-versus-ideation and attempt-versus-depressed interactions, but not attempt-versus-positive. The text then describes 'depression and positive episodes were flatter,' which conflicts with the stated significant differences and the non-significant attempt-positive comparison. The interpretation does not align cleanly with the reported contrasts.
issues.quote: self-focus tended to increase preceding an attempt, whereas depression and positive episodes were flatter and ideation appeared to show change over time in a downward direction.

issues.subcategory: discussion claims anxiety mean difference despite non-significant result
issues.description: The discussion states that high-risk periods were associated with greater anxiety and sadness, but the results table shows no significant fixed effect of episode type for anxiety (p=.306). This is a direct contradiction of the reported inferential results.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.

issues.subcategory: abstract overstates uniqueness of findings relative to results
issues.description: The abstract says anger increased and positive emotion decreased 'to a greater extent as one approached a suicide attempt,' implying unique attempt-specific effects. While those interactions were significant versus all episode types, other reported interactions (e.g., emotional tone, self-focus) were not unique; moreover, the small and selective attempt sample undermines strong wording. The abstract does not convey the fragility and multiplicity caveats emphasized later.
issues.quote: However, when examining patterns over time, anger increased and positive emotion decreased to a greater extent as one approached a suicide attempt.

issues.subcategory: multiple testing without correction despite exploratory analyses
issues.description: The study runs a large number of omnibus and pairwise tests across many outcomes and two analysis families, then explicitly declines any multiple-comparison adjustment. In a small pilot with many tests, this substantially elevates false-positive risk, especially for marginal p-values near .05 (e.g., .049, .046, .035). The Rothman citation does not eliminate the need to interpret familywise false discovery risk here.
issues.quote: Given this is a pilot study... we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.subcategory: post hoc time-window selection
issues.description: Although the study says the two-week window was chosen conservatively, it also states that the optimal window was assessed empirically via visual inspection of descriptive figures and that changes often occurred around 7 days before attempts. This indicates post hoc inspection of the same data to inform window choice, introducing researcher degrees of freedom and potential overfitting.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.subcategory: unclear preregistration status and deviations from a priori plan
issues.description: The paper says features were selected a priori and materials are on OSF, but it does not clearly state whether hypotheses and analysis plans were preregistered before examining the data, nor whether the exploratory alternate subset analyses and visual time-window assessments were prespecified. This limits the reader's ability to distinguish confirmatory from exploratory findings.
issues.quote: we analyzed and compared text messages during episodes within person based on a number of features selected a priori

issues.subcategory: power analysis not aligned with actual multilevel model
issues.description: The reported power analysis appears to be based on chi-square tests and design-effect simplifications, not on the actual generalized/linear mixed-effects models with complex nesting, unequal cluster sizes, and sparse key cells. The statement that 30 attempters would provide adequate power is not justified for the final analysis structure, especially given only 15 participants contributed attempt episodes with SMS data.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters... would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models comparing suicide attempts to other types of episodes

issues.subcategory: power calculation assumptions conflict with realized sample contributing attempt data
issues.description: The manuscript's power discussion assumes a sample size of 30 suicide attempters and references 20 with usable SMS data, but the realized analytic sample for attempt episodes appears to be 15 participants and 21 attempts with SMS data. This discrepancy means the already-approximate power calculation does not match the actual data analyzed.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters... representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data...

issues.subcategory: insufficient model specification details
issues.description: Critical details are missing for replication and evaluation: whether time was centered/scaled, whether slopes were allowed to vary by episode within participant, whether overdispersion or zero inflation was assessed for sparse word-count outcomes, how singular fits were handled, optimizer settings, and exact random-effects formulas. Merely stating 'maximal' or 'near-maximal' is insufficient.
issues.quote: a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes, was used... Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: questionable random intercept for message-level outcome
issues.description: The manuscript states that models included a random intercept of message, yet each message appears to contribute a single observation for a given outcome. A random intercept for a unique observational unit is generally unidentifiable/redundant and suggests confusion in model specification or reporting. If message IDs were unique, this component would absorb residual variance improperly or simply be non-estimable.
issues.quote: a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message

issues.subcategory: day treated as 'numerical factor' despite slope interpretation
issues.description: The manuscript describes day of episode as a 'numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0' while simultaneously interpreting linear changes over time (slopes). A factor-coded day and a numeric linear day variable are not the same model. This ambiguity is substantive because it changes the meaning of the interaction and pairwise contrasts.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: likely wrong endpoint count for 14-day window
issues.description: The study defines a two-week period but codes day from -14 to 0, which yields 15 values if inclusive. This creates ambiguity about the actual window length and whether the day of attempt was included. For a design centered on temporal proximity to attempts, such ambiguity affects replication and interpretation.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: insufficient handling/reporting of zero-word or very short messages
issues.description: Many text messages are likely extremely short or empty of analyzable words (e.g., 'ok', emojis, images). LIWC proportions and binomial representations can be unstable or undefined for messages with zero relevant tokens. The manuscript does not describe exclusion rules, preprocessing of emojis/nonwords, minimum word counts, or treatment of messages with zero words.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

issues.subcategory: episode windows may overlap or be nonindependent
issues.description: Participants could contribute up to three episodes per type, but the manuscript does not report whether episodes were required to be nonoverlapping in calendar time, whether the same texts could belong to multiple episodes, or how temporally adjacent episodes were handled. Overlap would violate assumptions and contaminate within-subject contrasts.
issues.quote: A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant depending on the presence and number of reported events. For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes

issues.subcategory: no details on blinding of interviewers/analysts
issues.description: The same study team collected the data, interviewed participants about episode types, and processed/analyzed messages. The manuscript does not report whether interviewers were blinded to hypotheses during episode elicitation, whether coders/analysts were blinded to episode labels during preprocessing, or whether any independent verification of dates/classifications occurred. This leaves room for bias in episode boundary assignment and data handling.
issues.quote: Recruitment and data collection were performed by J.J.G. A.L.N. and J.J.G. processed and formatted the data, and J.J.G. performed the data analysis

issues.subcategory: subjective confidence in date accuracy used in place of validation
issues.description: Participants' confidence ratings about recalled episode dates do not validate the actual accuracy of those dates. Given the analyses depend on exact day-by-day trajectories in the two weeks before attempts, even errors of a few days can materially distort slope estimates. The study lacks external validation of episode timing.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as ‘very certain’ (i.e., exact days) or ‘somewhat certain’ (i.e., may be off by a few days).

issues.subcategory: episodic risk hierarchy assumed rather than established
issues.description: The study treats attempt, ideation, depressed, and positive episodes as ordered risk levels (high, moderate, minimal/no risk), but these categories are heterogeneous and not necessarily linearly ordered in acute suicide risk across individuals. For example, some 'depressed/high stress' periods may be acutely risky, and some aborted attempts may not exceed severe ideation episodes. This weakens the conceptual basis of the comparisons.
issues.quote: In terms of suicide risk levels, attempt episodes were considered “high risk,” ideation episodes were considered “moderate risk,” and depressed and positive episodes were considered “minimal/no risk.”

issues.subcategory: misuse of 'biomarker' terminology
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly uses 'digital biomarkers' or 'biomarkers' for text-derived behavioral features. These are not biomarkers in the standard biomedical sense and have not been validated as stable biological or clinically actionable indicators. The terminology overstates what the measures represent.
issues.quote: we aimed to utilize ecological private SMS data to gain insight into possible novel, real-time digital biomarkers of suicidal behaviors.

issues.subcategory: theoretical mechanisms inferred from associative language markers
issues.description: The discussion interprets language patterns as clues to the 'suicidal mind' and as reflecting activation or affective changes leading to attempts. But the observed text changes could be driven by many confounders associated with crises, interpersonal conflict, substance use, or context of texting rather than suicide risk per se. The design does not isolate mechanisms.
issues.quote: Overall, these results indicate that a small set of specific private text communication habits, particularly tied to use of emotional language, potentially provide clues into the suicidal mind

issues.subcategory: no control for obvious time-varying confounds
issues.description: Within-subject designs reduce stable between-person confounding but do not address time-varying confounds such as day of week, semester timing, holidays, relationship events, alcohol/drug use, treatment changes, or major stressors that could influence texting behavior and emotion language. None are modeled or controlled, despite being highly plausible alternative explanations for the observed trajectories.
issues.quote: we quantitatively compared whether and in what ways their text messages from periods of acute suicide risk... differed from other periods

issues.subcategory: lack of episode counts by type in analytic sample
issues.description: The paper reports total episodes and episodes with SMS data but does not clearly report the number of analyzable episodes by each type in the main analyses. Because the key contrasts depend on sparse attempt episodes, readers cannot adequately assess balance, precision, or contribution of each episode type.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.subcategory: effect size reporting is inappropriate/unclear
issues.description: The paper states that β values in log-odds units are 'standardized' and serve as effect sizes. Raw logistic coefficients are not standardized effect sizes, and in mixed models their comparability across outcomes is limited. This could mislead readers about the magnitude and interpretability of effects.
issues.quote: Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.subcategory: no confidence intervals for key estimates
issues.description: The results provide p-values and some coefficients/SEs but no confidence intervals for primary effects or pairwise contrasts. CIs are especially important in a small pilot with sparse data to convey uncertainty and avoid dichotomous interpretation of marginal findings.
issues.quote: Pairwise comparisons revealed that attempt episodes were significantly higher in sad words compared to ideation (z=2.64, p=.008)

issues.subcategory: table note conflicts with near-significant pairwise practices and omitted estimates
issues.description: Table notes say pairwise comparisons were performed only for significant fixed effects/interactions, yet the paper also discusses nonsignificant pairwise patterns and omits some model estimates for nonsignificant omnibus tests. This selective reporting makes it difficult to evaluate whether omitted contrasts were planned and whether interpretation is cherry-picked.
issues.quote: Note. Pairwise comparisons performed only for significant fixed effects

issues.subcategory: selective emphasis on significant interactions from many tested variables
issues.description: The manuscript tests numerous LIWC outcomes and then foregrounds a small set of significant interactions (positive emotion, anger, self-focus) as evidence of potential markers. In the absence of correction, preregistration, or external validation, this creates substantial risk that highlighted findings are sample-specific chance results.
issues.quote: Unique to attempts, positive emotion decreased and anger increased to a greater extent as one approached a suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous data extraction methods across devices
issues.description: Different software and apps were used across iPhone and Android devices, with acknowledged failures for some encrypted iPhones. Extraction heterogeneity can affect completeness, formatting, metadata, and message recoverability. The manuscript does not report validation that extraction methods yielded comparable data quality across platforms.
issues.quote: participants with iPhones were instructed to download their SMS text messages using software programs called iExplorer, SynciOS Manager, and SynciOS Data Recovery, and those with Android devices were instructed to download their messages using Android mobile apps called SMS Backup & Restore and SMS to Text.

issues.subcategory: SMS-only communication may not reflect participants' main communication channels
issues.description: Especially in young adults, SMS may be only one component of digital communication, with substantial migration to apps such as Snapchat, WhatsApp, Instagram, etc. Thus, the available SMS corpus may be an incomplete and nonrepresentative sample of interpersonal communication during episodes, limiting inference about 'private electronic communication' more broadly.
issues.quote: Additional forms of personal digital data... were collected for the purposes of future analyses but are not part of the current study.

issues.subcategory: insufficient description of text preprocessing decisions
issues.description: The paper does not explain how group texts, attachments, duplicates, timestamps, timezone issues, non-English messages, autocorrect artifacts, emoticons, and punctuation-only messages were handled. Such preprocessing choices can materially affect LIWC scores and daily aggregates.
issues.quote: participants’ SMS data files were individually cleaned using Python to standardize the encoding of messages and naming of variables across all participants.

issues.subcategory: clinical utility claims exceed evidence
issues.description: The discussion suggests the work could lead to objective monitoring tools that notify clinicians or family based on communication patterns. Yet no predictive performance metrics, calibration, false positive burden, or prospective validation are presented for the current analyses. Translational claims are therefore substantially premature.
issues.quote: Knowledge gained from this study could put us one step closer to the development of an objective monitoring tool capable of tracking individuals’ communication “behind the scenes,” notifying suicidal individuals and/or their clinician or family

issues.subcategory: claim of first study on private text messaging and mental health is likely overstated
issues.description: The manuscript claims this is the first study to examine private text messaging and mental health outcomes 'suicide or otherwise,' which is an expansive assertion unlikely to be supportable and not necessary for the argument. Overstated novelty can mislead readers about prior literature context.
issues.quote: This is the first research study, to our knowledge, to examine the association between private text messaging data and mental health outcomes, suicide or otherwise.
